text: The Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves of 1807 (2 Stat. 426, enacted March 2, 1807) is a United States federal law that bans the importation of enslaved people into the United States, taking effect on January 1, 1808—the earliest date allowed by the U.S. Constitution. President Thomas Jefferson advocated for the law, calling for its enactment in his 1806 State of the Union Address, and had supported the idea since the 1770s. The law built upon earlier efforts, including the Slave Trade Act of 1794, which prohibited American ships from participating in the international slave trade, and the 1800 Act, which banned U.S. citizens from investing in or working on slave-trading ships. The 1807 law went further by criminalizing the importation of slaves from abroad, even on foreign vessels. It did not affect the domestic slave trade, which grew in importance after the end of imported slaves, and some smuggling continued. The law applied only to importation and exportation of enslaved people, not internal trade between states. Article 1, Section 9 of the Constitution had protected states' participation in the Atlantic slave trade for twenty years, and this provision could not be altered by constitutional amendment, meaning federal prohibition could only begin on January 1, 1808. While all Thirteen Colonies had banned the international slave trade during the American Revolution, some states later reopened it: North Carolina banned imports in 1794 and strengthened the ban in 1795; Georgia allowed the trade until 1798; and South Carolina reopened the trade in December 1803, importing 39,075 enslaved people between 1804 and 1808. By 1807, only South Carolina allowed the Atlantic slave trade. The Migration or Importation of such Persons as any of the States now existing shall think proper to admit, shall not be prohibited by the Congress prior to the Year one thousand eight hundred and eight, but a tax or duty may be imposed on such Importation, not exceeding ten dollars for each Person. Historians estimate that up to 50,000 enslaved people were illegally imported after 1808, mostly through Spanish Florida and Texas, and South Carolina Governor Henry Middleton estimated 13,000 smuggled African slaves arrived annually in 1819. The 1808 law spurred demand for fast vessels, with records indicating seven slavers were regularly fitted out in New York as late as 1859 and many more in major ports. In 1820, slave trading became a capital offense, with 74 cases prosecuted between 1837 and 1860, though few captains were convicted and only Nathaniel Gordon, hanged in 1862, was executed. After 1808, many Americans continued the slave trade by transporting Africans to Cuba, with nearly one-third of all slave ships between 1808 and 1860 owned by American merchants or built and outfitted in American ports, and it is possible U.S. citizens transported twice as many Africans to Cuba and Brazil as to U.S. ports. The U.S. Navy delayed anti-slaving patrols, only gaining authority in 1820, and enforcement was sporadic and ineffective; U.S. ships falsely flew the American flag to evade British patrols, and the first U.S. warship sent to intercept slavers was the USS Cyane, which arrested 11 American slavers in 1820–1821. No further patrols occurred until 1842, when they were limited by political pressure from slave-owning states. The Atlantic slave trade was not fully ended until the U.S. Civil War, when American-built and -managed ships were barred from operating. In the South, the Fire-Eaters—pro-slavery extremists—called for repealing the 1807 law and legalizing the international slave trade, viewing it as a way to assert the morality of slavery, drive down slave prices, balance Northern immigration, and maintain Southern congressional representation. They believed that if slavery was morally acceptable, then the slave trade must be too, a view that alarmed even pro-slavery figures like former President John Tyler, who condemned the proposal. As cotton prices rose in the 1850s, demand for enslaved labor increased, leading to calls to reopen the trade to meet demand or lower prices. While some Southerners opposed the idea, the general sentiment supported reopening the trade as a logical extension of pro-slavery ideology. Conventions of Southern planters repeatedly urged the re-opening, but such efforts failed in Congress, and state attempts to allow the importation of "apprentices" from Africa were unsuccessful. When repeal failed, some ignored the law, with notable cases including the smuggling of enslaved people aboard the Wanderer and the Clotilda.
